transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-02-27
Start: 16:00 PST
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Arjun Patel (Redwood SE), Liam O'Neill (Horizon AI - Head of ML), Priya Rao (Product), Marcus Lee (Infra), Sofia (intern)

Summary (auto-generated): Quick walkthrough of JSON mode, guardrails and operator controls. Demo included an example of a multi-step agent calling an internal ticketing tool and a calendar tool via function call emulation. Discussed PoC next steps and security docs.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya with Redwood, and with me is Arjun, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:00:08] Liam O'Neill: Good, thanks. Excited to see how the structured output stuff works — we've been trying to reduce hallucinated ticket fields in our internal agent.
[00:00:15] Priya Rao: Hi, quick intro, I'm Priya, product; mainly interested in guardrails and the Console UX for non-ML folks.
[00:00:22] Marcus Lee: Marcus here, infra. We'll want details on VPC, key management, and latency.
[00:00:27] Maya Chen: Awesome. Agenda: quick context + goals, Arjun will demo JSON mode and function calling with schema enforcement, then we'll show Console rollout controls and Optimize recommendations, and finish with Q/A and next steps. Does that sound good?
[00:00:40] Liam O'Neill: Yep. Our big win criteria: structured outputs that are strong enough to feed downstream systems without a heavy sanitization layer, and predictable latency under load.
[00:00:50] Arjun Patel: Cool, jumping in. I'm going to share my screen — showing the Redwood API playground first. A note on terminology — "JSON mode" here is Redwood's structured output mode where you provide a JSON schema and the model is biased/tuned to produce compliant output; we also have runtime validators that can run post-generation.
[00:01:10] Arjun Patel: (screen) So here's a sample schema for a support ticket: {"title": "string", "priority": "enum[low,medium,high]", "customer_id": "string", "created_at": "iso8601", "actions": [{"type":"enum[assign,escalate,close]","target":"string"}]} — obviously transcription might mangle braces but the concept is there.
[00:01:34] Priya Rao: Can the schema express nested required fields?
[00:01:37] Arjun Patel: Yes, you can mark fields required, nested arrays and object types are supported. We also support regex patterns for IDs and custom validators you can register.
[00:01:48] Liam O'Neill: What happens if the model spits out malformed JSON — does Redwood auto-correct or reject?
[00:01:52] Arjun Patel: Good question. There are layered behaviors: first we bias sampling to prefer schema-conforming tokens. If the model still outputs invalid JSON, our post-processor will try two things: 1) a best-effort repair (e.g., fix trailing commas, close braces) up to configured heuristics; 2) if repair fails or doesn't pass strict validation, the runtime can either emit an error or fall back to a secondary model variant or return a string that indicates failure. You can configure policies per route.
[00:02:18] Marcus Lee: Any measurable latency for strict mode vs permissive?
[00:02:22] Arjun Patel: In our benchmarks, strict validation and best-effort repair adds roughly 10-40ms in the happy path. If you enable full JSON parsing and custom validators, it can be 20-80ms depending on payload size. But these are post-token costs — the token generation is still the main cost. We have Optimize suggestions on the Console to trade off strictness vs throughput.
[00:02:42] Maya Chen: Let's do a live demo. Arjun, run the sample agent that calls two functions: 1) create_ticket (internal API) and 2) calendar_invite (Google Calendar style). Make sure the schema for create_ticket has required fields and an actions array.
[00:02:56] Arjun Patel: Starting demo — sending prompt: "User report: 'App crashes on save with error code 0x77f' — create a ticket and schedule a triage meeting." The model responds with structured JSON that maps to our schema.
[00:03:12] (audio glitch) [00:03:12] Speaker 1: ---
[00:03:15] Arjun Patel: Ok transcript shows returned JSON: 
{"title": "Crash on save - error 0x77f","priority":"high","customer_id":"hzn-9987","created_at":"2025-02-27T23:12:04Z","actions":[{"type":"assign","target":"oncall-team"},{"type":"escalate","target":"eng-lead"}]}
[00:03:35] Arjun Patel: The runtime then calls create_ticket with that payload and returns a ticket id. Next the agent invoked calendar_invite with fields: participants, start_time, duration, subject.
[00:03:47] Priya Rao: Nice. How do you map those function calls to our internal endpoints? We have an internal ticketing API with slightly different field names.
[00:03:52] Arjun Patel: You map via a simple adapter. In Redwood Console you can define a function schema and provide a transformation layer (a small mapping script or template) that converts the generated JSON to your API payload. We also support direct webhook-style function endpoints so the runtime can POST to your endpoint in a VPC-private network if using Private deployment.
[00:04:10] Marcus Lee: VPC/private network — can you detail that? We can't expose internal endpoints publicly.
[00:04:15] Maya Chen: Absolutely. For Redwood Private we install a customer-managed control plane and a connector that lives in your VPC, so function calls can be routed inside your network. KMS/HSM integration for key material is supported; we tie audit logs back to the control plane. We'll share the architecture diagram after the call.
[00:04:31] Liam O'Neill: Another question — what about tool calling with multiple steps and failure modes? E.g., create_ticket succeeds but calendar_invite fails. We want clear, machine-readable error states.
[00:04:41] Arjun Patel: We return structured responses for tool outcomes as well: {"status":"ok|error","error_code":"string","error_message":"string","result":{...}} — plus we emit events to the Console traces. You can set retry policies per function and fallback policies (e.g., notify a human, queue a retry, or call a lower-capacity model).
[00:05:00] Priya Rao: Is it possible to have the model call a human-in-the-loop step when confidence is low?
[00:05:04] Arjun Patel: Yes, you can set confidence thresholds based on logits or custom scoring. When below threshold, runtime can create a task for an operator or return a structured "review_required" signal.
[00:05:13] [00:05:14] Sofia: (soft) How do you prevent data leakage in function payloads — like PII in the actions array?
[00:05:19] Arjun Patel: You can define field-level redaction policies in the schema — mark fields as pii:true and Redwood will obfuscate or hash those fields before sending to any downstream tool unless the endpoint is explicitly allowed in the policy.
[00:05:30] Maya Chen: Now switching to Console — showing rollout controls. You can create a route, pin a model variant, and attach a rollout policy with canary percentage, rollback thresholds for error rates and latency SLOs.
[00:05:42] Arjun Patel: (screen) On the left, route config. Here we have "support-agent-route" with JSON mode enabled, schema attached, and function mappings. We set canary to 10% traffic for 24 hours with automated alerting if schema failure rate > 1% or 99th percentile latency > 500ms.
[00:05:59] Liam O'Neill: Can the canary be weighted by customer or token type? Our power users generate longer contexts.
[00:06:04] Arjun Patel: Yes, routing policies can match by header, customer_tier, or any request attribute. You can also set sequence length buckets and route heavy long-seq requests to a variant optimized for long contexts.
[00:06:14] Marcus Lee: About Optimize recommendations — can you show how Redwood suggests batching or quantization?
[00:06:18] Arjun Patel: Sure — open Optimize tab. We run a simulated workload analysis based on a sample of your prompts (you can upload a small prompt set). Optimize will recommend an execution profile: batch size, max tokens per batch, KV cache policy, and quantization level per model to meet target latency and reduce cost.
[00:06:34] Priya Rao: Is the quantization recommendation tied to output quality evaluation? We don't want regressions.
[00:06:38] Arjun Patel: Yes, Optimize reports expected quality delta and runs a small set of evals on your prompt set. You can set tolerances (e.g., <1% drop in extraction accuracy) and the recommendation will respect that.
[00:06:50] Liam O'Neill: How do we evaluate extraction accuracy? We have labeled tickets.
[00:06:54] Arjun Patel: Upload a labeled test set to Console Evals. We'll run model variants and produce per-field precision/recall charts and regression alerts. It's how we caught structured-output regressions in past customers.
[00:07:06] (short pause)
[00:07:09] Maya Chen: Some items to call out: you can run Redwood in Hosted mode to get started fast, then move to Dedicated or Private for isolation and predictable SLAs. For your use-case — heavy customer PII and internal endpoints — Private is likely the path.
[00:07:24] Liam O'Neill: Cost wise, how much more does Private run compared to hosted? ballpark?
[00:07:29] Maya Chen: Private has a platform fee plus infra commit; it depends on capacity. Arjun, do you have a sizing example?
[00:07:34] Arjun Patel: For a small Dedicated cluster supporting ~50 QPS with 2x redundancy, typical monthly costs in our benchmarks are comparable to a mid-tier cloud GPU commit. We'll send an estimate tailored to your QPS and model selection.
[00:07:47] Priya Rao: Can we see logs / tracing for schema failures?
[00:07:50] Arjun Patel: Console has per-request traces and a schema-failure dashboard. Each failure record includes the generated payload, validation error, model variant, and upstream request metadata (IP masked).
[00:08:01] Marcus Lee: About compliance — we need SOC 2 + ISO artifacts, pen test reports, and an incidence response workflow.
[00:08:08] Maya Chen: We'll share the standard security pack and a tailored slide for Private deployment that describes audit logs and incident response. We'll also loop in our Security lead.
[00:08:16] Liam O'Neill: Ok good. Back to JSON mode specifics — what about partial fields and defaulting? Like if user doesn't give customer_id, can we infer?
[00:08:25] Arjun Patel: You can mark fields as optional and provide enrichment hooks. For example, a 'lookup_customer' enrichment function that runs if customer_id missing. Enrichers are executed as pre-processing steps and can call your internal DB (again, only within VPC for Private).
[00:08:40] Priya Rao: Does Console let product folks create/modify schemas without heavy engineering?
[00:08:44] Arjun Patel: Yes — we have a Schema Editor in Console with validation and preview mode. Non-technical users can toggle required flags and preview sample outputs. For complex validators you can attach a small JS validator snippet.
[00:08:57] Marcus Lee: A security question: if a schema contains a PII field and someone with lower RBAC tries to download logs, can we redact?
[00:09:03] Arjun Patel: RBAC is field-aware. You can set roles that can view raw payloads; others get masked versions. All actions are audited.
[00:09:11] Liam O'Neill: Great. Let's talk about failure modes — say the model returns an action type not in enum, but it's still parseable. What's the policy?
[00:09:19] Arjun Patel: That's a validation error. Policy can be set to coerce (map unknown enum to 'other' and attach original string), reject (error out), or fallback to a mapper function you control. We logged a case study in the docs — we'll share link.
[00:09:33] Priya Rao: For our product flow, we need structured audit trails for each step. Does Redwood tie events to user identities?
[00:09:39] Maya Chen: Yes, audit logs include request-level metadata including user id, route, model version, schema version, function calls and result statuses. For Private, logs can be stored in your S3 or forwarded to your SIEM.
[00:09:51] (screen-change)
[00:09:53] Arjun Patel: Quick demo of a canary rollback — I change rollout threshold to 0.5% schema failures and simulate traffic that pushes failure to 1.2%. The Console auto-rolls back to previous model variant and triggers Slack and PagerDuty hooks.
[00:10:08] (customer murmurs)
[00:10:12] Liam O'Neill: That's useful. For the PoC, we want benchmark numbers: tail latencies at 95/99, schema-failure rate, cost per 1k tickets. Can you provide that?
[00:10:20] Arjun Patel: We'll run a focused benchmark using your sample prompt set and provide a report with those metrics. We'll also include recommendations on batching and caching.
[00:10:29] Priya Rao: One last UX question — how does a product owner inspect failed payloads and re-run them after fixes?
[00:10:35] Arjun Patel: There's an Events page. You can filter failures, open the record, edit the generated JSON (or script a transformation), and re-run the function call in a sandbox environment. Re-runs are tagged and audited.
[00:10:47] Sofia: (soft) Are there rate limits across function calls to stop accidental storms?
[00:10:51] Arjun Patel: Yes per-route rate limiting and per-function quotas. You can set soft limits that throttle and hard limits that reject. Also cost alerts.
[00:11:00] Maya Chen: Alright, quick recap — agreed PoC: Redwood runs 1-week baseline against Horizon sample prompts, provide latency/throughput, schema-failure stats, and Optimize recommendations. We'll send security pack and JSON schema templates. Horizon to provide sample prompts and expected SLOs.
[00:11:16] Liam O'Neill: Sounds good. Any concerns on our side — Marcus?
[00:11:20] Marcus Lee: Mostly network and keys — need to see the connector diagram and how HSM integration looks.
[00:11:24] Maya Chen: We'll include an architecture diagram and the HSM/KMS integration steps.
[00:11:28] (small chatter)
[00:11:33] Priya Rao: One more nit — are there SDKs in Go and Python for function definition and client-side validation?
[00:11:38] Arjun Patel: Yes Go, Python, TypeScript. SDKs include client-side validators that can validate schema before request, saving a round trip.
[00:11:47] Liam O'Neill: Great. Any competitors we should be aware of?
[00:11:49] Maya Chen: Customers often compare us to Anthropic and OpenAI-standard APIs for simplicity and to Lambda Labs for self-host. But Redwood differentiates on routable, observable inference with guardrails and Private deployment options.
[00:12:01] (pause)
[00:12:06] Maya Chen: Ok wrapping — we'll follow up with an email covering: PoC scope, timeline, pricing ballpark, security pack, and the JSON schema templates. Any final questions?
[00:12:18] Liam O'Neill: No, thanks. Looking forward to the PoC.
[00:12:21] Priya Rao: Thanks everyone.
[00:12:23] Maya Chen: Thanks all — I'll send notes and next steps.

(remaining 36 minutes: call included deeper Q/A and an extended demo where Arjun showed:
- Console Schema Editor and a preview generator with a "fuzz test" button that runs 500 synthetic inputs to estimate failure rate,
- A code snippet in the SDK showing function registration: register_function("create_ticket", schema, endpoint, {"retry":2, "timeout_ms":3000}),
- Demo of a repair heuristic where the model returned single quotes and a missing comma; the runtime applied a repair rule then re-validated,
- A trace view showing a failed canary rollout that auto-rolled back and created a Jira ticket via a webhook,
- Optimize dashboard showing recommended quantization "int8-p4" for a model variant with expected cost savings ~28% and quality delta -0.6% on the extraction metrics.
)

End of meeting.
